source.title: REINFORCE Adversarial Attacks on Large Language Models: An Adaptive, Distributional, and Semantic Objective
source.authors: Simon Geisler; Tom Wollschlager; M. H. I. Abdalla; Vincent Cohen-Addad; Johannes Gasteiger; Stephan Gunnemann

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffix attacks can elicit harmful responses from aligned models, using adaptive REINFORCE attacks and harmful-response rates rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: Reports harmful-response attack success rates for affirmative-objective and REINFORCE suffix attacks, plus a circuit-breaker setting and a single example where a likely affirmative opening is followed harmlessly. Other attack-method and sampling ablations are not included unless they bear directly on harmful-completion rates. The paper’s prompts and its warning about upsetting appendix content are not instructions addressed to an AI reviewer.
record.test_reason: Optimized adversarial suffixes and prompts (GCG, PGD) are run against safety-trained models, with HarmBench harmful-response rates as the measure. This bears on V4's suffix clause. It is a different method from the originals' prefilling and token-position analyses. The paper also argues that making a compliant opening likely does not by itself yield harmful completions, which qualifies V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that maximizing a fixed affirmative opening is an inconsistent objective. The model can start compliantly yet finish harmlessly, so affirmative-objective attacks overestimate robustness. An adaptive, distributional, semantic REINFORCE objective roughly doubles ASR on Llama 2/3 and breaks circuit breakers (2% to 23% full set, 50% on a subset).
record.recipe_differences: Uses test-time adversarial prompt optimization (GCG and PGD), not fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, parameter localization, or training to deepen safety.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies across models and GCG versus PGD. The circuit-breaker result varies with seed choice and prompt subset. Evaluation uses greedy generations and ASR@512; the authors note that judge choice and evaluation length can affect results.
record.problems: Evaluation reports a single trial per prompt. Harmfulness is judged by an LLM judge, which the authors note is imperfect. Evaluation scores greedy generations, which the authors say may not represent other sampling outputs and may be unstable. The 50% circuit-breaker result is on a selected subset of prompts.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant result rows omitted.

untested.parts: All; no per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Direct prefilling of compliant tokens and decoding changes. Only optimized suffix/prefix prompts are tested, and no unattacked baseline ASR is reported in the paper.
No deepening training. Circuit breakers are attacked, but the paper does not frame them as spreading safety beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: AdvPrefix (model-specific prefilling-derived targets) results. Affirmative objective: 0.70 Llama 3 / 0.14 circuit breaker. REINFORCE: 0.81 / 0.48 (ASR@512). Shows that even optimized compliant openings leave circuit breakers mostly intact.
Qualitative observation that models sometimes refuse in their first sentences but ultimately provide the harmful answer under attack.
ASR@128 results for GCG, e.g. REINFORCE on Vicuna 1.00 and on Llama 2 0.63.

record.verdict_notes: The paper reports no no-attack (direct request) ASR, so every row lacks a true control. Rows' baselines compare two attack objectives, which is the study's own method versus a prior one. Vicuna 1.5 has minimal safety tuning, so its rows say little about safety-trained models. The circuit-breaker rows concern a defense acting beyond the opening tokens. They could inform V7-style 'does a deeper defense hold up' questions, but the paper does not frame them that way, so they are left on V4 only. The r24 finding cuts against a strong reading of V4: securing the compliant opening did not bypass safety in that example.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning with harmful examples and its effect on safety.
Fine-tuning with benign data and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Tests optimized adversarial suffixes, not direct prefill of compliant tokens or decoding changes.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and testing whether it remains robust.

relationships.condition: Gemma 1.1 2B/7B, Llama 3 8B and Vicuna 1.5 7B under GCG or PGD suffix attacks with the REINFORCE objective
relationships.reason: Harmful-response rates reach 0.69–0.95 on HarmBench standard behaviors (r2, r4, r8, r10, r12, r14, r18, r20). Affirmative-objective attacks on the Gemma and Vicuna models also exceed 0.5 (r1, r3, r9, r11, r13, r19).
relationships.display_finding: Harmful-response rates reached 0.69–0.95 on HarmBench standard behaviors, and affirmative-objective attacks on the Gemma and Vicuna models also exceeded 0.5.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Gemma 1.1 2B/7B, Llama 3 8B and Vicuna 1.5 7B under GCG or PGD suffix attacks with the REINFORCE objective
source_check.reason: The group mixes near-full bypass on Gemma/Vicuna with incomplete Llama 3 results (r8=0.73; r18=0.69), requiring separate condition groups. Affirmative Gemma results are also partial. PGD optimizes both a prefix and suffix, so its results do not establish suffix-only efficacy.

relationships.condition: Llama 2 7B, and Llama 3 8B under the affirmative objective
relationships.reason: Suffix attacks defeat refusal on only 17–57% of behaviors, and the result depends on attack method and objective (r5, r6, r7, r15, r16, r17).
relationships.display_finding: Suffix attacks defeated refusal on only 17–57% of behaviors, depending on attack method and objective.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Llama 2 7B, and Llama 3 8B under the affirmative objective
source_check.reason: r5–r7 and r15–r17 show incomplete bypass dependent on model, attack and objective. The cited values are correct, although their actual range is 17–57%, with the REINFORCE-GCG value for Llama 2 equal to 56%.

relationships.reason: Affirmative GCG almost never succeeds (2%, r21). REINFORCE reaches 23% on the full set (r22) and 50% only on a selected subset with a history seed (r23).
relationships.display_finding: Affirmative GCG succeeded only 2% of the time. REINFORCE reached 23% on the full set and 50% only on a selected subset with a history seed.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r21–r23 show strong dependence on objective, seed and prompt selection: 2% affirmative GCG, 23% REINFORCE with affirmative seed, and 50% with history seed on the explicitly selected subset.

relationships.condition: Affirmative-opening targeting (fixed compliant start), Gemma 1.1 7B example
relationships.reason: A suffix made the compliant opening >60% likely, yet the completion stayed harmless (r24). The authors state this happens 'frequently'; this rests on text, not a measured rate.
relationships.display_finding: A suffix made the compliant opening more than 60% likely, yet the completion stayed harmless. The authors say this happens frequently but give no measured rate.

source_check.condition: Affirmative-opening targeting (fixed compliant start), Gemma 1.1 7B example
source_check.reason: For this single illustrated condition, r24 explicitly shows the bypass effect absent: the targeted opening exceeds 60% likelihood but the completion is harmless. This is a qualitative counterexample, not a measured failure rate or a direct forced-prefill experiment.
